questions.stem: Intertextual references only 'work' as a meaning-making device when:
options: the audience recognises the earlier text being referred to
the earlier text is more recent than the text making the reference
the creator names the earlier text openly somewhere in the new text
the two texts belong to exactly the same medium and genre
questions.explanation: An allusion adds a layer of meaning only if viewers or listeners bring knowledge of the original text with them; without recognition, the reference passes unnoticed and the extra layer is lost. The option about naming the source openly is the most tempting, but most intertextual references are unstated — a visual echo or sampled riff — and naming them would often destroy the effect. Test recognition, not acknowledgement.
questions.teaching:
References to other texts depend on something outside the text itself.

The device works by borrowing meaning from an earlier work — its associations, its tone, what readers already feel about it. That borrowed meaning only arrives if the reader has the earlier text available to recognise. Where they do not, the reference is simply invisible: the text still makes sense, but a layer is lost. This is why writers choose references to works their intended audience is likely to share, and why some references age badly.

questions.stem: A charity poster shows an ordinary volunteer standing in the same pose as a famous statue of a heroic figure. The most likely purpose of this visual intertextual reference is to:
options: show the audience that the poster was photographed in an art gallery
warn the audience that the image has been digitally manipulated
transfer ideas of heroism and strength onto the everyday volunteer
prove that the charity has legal permission to use famous artworks
questions.explanation: Visual allusion works by association: quoting the composition of a well-known heroic image invites viewers to read the volunteer through the values already attached to that image. The gallery-setting option misreads the reference as literal information about where the photo was taken, when the pose itself is the borrowed element, not the location. When a familiar composition reappears, ask what values travel across with it.

questions.stem: A short film opens with a shot of a lone figure in a doorway framed by desert light, closely echoing the ending of a classic Western. For a viewer who knows the Western, this opening most likely:
options: guarantees that the short film will end with the same events as the Western
proves the short film was directed by the same filmmaker as the Western
tells the viewer that the short film is set in the same historical period
raises expectations about isolation and belonging before any dialogue occurs
questions.explanation: An intertextual opening shot layers the earlier film's associations — here, the outsider who cannot come inside — onto the new story, priming expectations before the narrative begins. The option that the film must end the same way is tempting but false: allusion borrows associations, and filmmakers frequently invoke a reference in order to subvert it. Treat a visual echo as a suggestion of meaning, not a plot guarantee.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the clearest example of intertextuality in a music video?
options: Using a handheld camera so the footage appears shaky and unplanned
Recreating the costumes and choreography of a famous 1980s video in new footage
Cutting rapidly between shots so the edits land on the beat of the song
Filming the whole video in black and white with a high-contrast look
questions.explanation: Intertextuality requires a link to a specific identifiable text, and recreating a recognisable video's costumes and choreography points directly at that earlier work. Editing to the beat is tempting because it is a deliberate technique, but it is a general stylistic convention used across thousands of videos and refers to no particular text. Ask: could I name the text being referred to? If not, it is style, not intertextuality.

questions.stem: An advertisement copies the lighting, music and slow-motion of a famous sports film, but the 'athlete' is a tired parent hanging out washing. The intertextual reference here mainly works by:
options: creating humour through the gap between the grand original and the mundane subject
removing all serious meaning from the original sports film for future audiences
making the advertisement harder to understand for its intended audience
proving that domestic tasks are physically as demanding as elite sport
questions.explanation: Parody depends on incongruity: the audience holds the borrowed epic style and the ordinary subject in mind at once, and the mismatch produces the humour and the affectionate point about everyday effort. The option about domestic tasks being as demanding as elite sport misreads a comic exaggeration as a literal factual claim the advertisement is proving. The cue for parody is a serious form applied to an unexpectedly small subject.

questions.stem: A documentary about a modern protest layers archival radio audio from a historic protest underneath present-day footage. The strongest analysis of this multimodal intertextual choice is that it:
options: confirms that the two protests were organised by the same group of people
functions as evidence that the historical protest achieved its stated aims
shows the filmmaker had no present-day audio available for the footage
invites viewers to read the current protest as continuing an earlier struggle
questions.explanation: Placing historic audio against contemporary images creates a deliberate juxtaposition, and the audience reads the two as connected, so the present event is framed as part of an ongoing history. The claim that the protests were organised by the same people is tempting because the sound feels like documentary proof, but layered archival audio is a rhetorical and editing choice, not evidence about organisers. When modes are combined from different eras, analyse the relationship the combination suggests, not a literal fact.

questions.stem: In media study, an 'intertextual reference' is best defined as:
options: a reference list of the sources a filmmaker used while researching the text
any repeated image or sound motif that appears more than once inside a single text
a direct quotation of dialogue spoken by a character to another character
a deliberate echo of another text, so meaning from that text is carried into the new one
questions.explanation: Intertextuality means one text pointing to another text — through image, sound, wording or style — so that the audience's knowledge of the first text adds meaning to the second. The option about a repeated motif inside a single text is tempting because repetition does build meaning, but that is internal patterning, not intertextuality: the reference must reach outside the text. The cue is the prefix 'inter-' — between texts, not within one.

questions.stem: A still image in a news article shows a group of workers arranged like the figures in a famous painting of a shared meal. The clearest effect of this composition is that it:
options: lends the everyday scene the dignity and significance the audience associates with the painting
proves the photographer physically staged the workers rather than photographing them candidly
tells the reader the article is about art history rather than about working conditions
removes any need for a caption because the image now explains itself completely
questions.explanation: Borrowing a famous composition transfers the tone and status of the original artwork onto the new subject, so ordinary workers are framed as significant. The staging option is tempting because such an echo often does involve arrangement, but the question asks about the effect on meaning, and staging is a production claim the image alone cannot prove. Separate 'how it was made' from 'what it means'.

questions.stem: A public health campaign runs a still image echoing a famous war-recruitment poster, with the pointing figure and bold slab lettering kept intact. A critic argues the choice is risky. The strongest reason for that judgement is that:
options: the borrowed poster carries associations of conflict and duty that may sit awkwardly with a health message
still images are unable to make intertextual references, so the campaign has used the wrong mode
the campaign should have used original artwork, because referencing another text is never persuasive
audiences only respond to moving images, so a still reference will not be noticed at all
questions.explanation: Intertextual references import the whole context of the source, including connotations a creator may not want, so a wartime poster can bring pressure and coercion into a health campaign. The claim that referencing is never persuasive is tempting if you distrust borrowing, but references are widely and effectively used; the risk lies in unwanted associations, not in borrowing itself. Always ask what else comes along with the borrowed image.

questions.stem: When a film uses a snippet of a well-known orchestral theme from an earlier movie, this is best described as an intertextual reference carried through:
options: the written captions of the text
the camera movement of the text
the sound elements of the text
the still image elements of the text
questions.explanation: Intertextual references can be made through any mode, and a borrowed musical theme is carried by sound (music and audio) rather than by picture or words. Naming 'the camera movement' is tempting because film feels visual, but the reference here is heard, not seen — camera movement would only carry a reference if a distinctive shot style were copied. The cue is to ask which mode the audience actually receives the borrowed material in: eyes, ears or text on screen.
questions.teaching:
A multimodal text carries meaning through several channels at once, and a reference to another text can be made through any of them.

The channels include written language, spoken language, still images, moving images, layout, and sound — music, effects and silence. So an echo of an earlier work does not have to be a quotation: a borrowed camera angle works visually, and a few bars of a recognisable theme works through what the audience hears. Identifying which channel is carrying the reference is what these questions test.

questions.stem: A sports drink advertisement uses a slow zoom onto a cracked trophy while a famous line from a Shakespeare tragedy is spoken in voiceover. What does the sound reference add that the image alone does not?
options: Factual information about how the trophy came to be cracked
A guarantee that the advertisement is aimed at older audiences only
Proof that the advertisement is based on a true sporting event
A sense of grand, tragic seriousness attached to the athlete's loss
questions.explanation: The borrowed line imports the tone and emotional scale of tragedy, so an ordinary sporting setback is framed as something weighty and dramatic. Saying it gives factual information about the trophy is wrong: quoted dialogue from another text explains nothing about the events on screen, it only colours how we feel about them. Ask what mood the reference brings, not what facts it supplies.

questions.stem: A film soundtrack, a poster's font choice and a video game's camera angles can all carry intertextual references. What does this show about intertextuality?
options: It can be built into any mode — visual, audio or written — not just the words of a text
It works only through spoken or written quotations that an audience can hear or read
It exists only when one text names the earlier text directly on screen
It appears only in moving images, because still images cannot refer to other texts
questions.explanation: Intertextual references are made whenever one text borrows recognisable features of another, and those features can be visual (composition, colour, costume), aural (music, sound effects, accents) or verbal (quoted lines). The tempting choice is the one limiting intertextuality to spoken or written quotations — but a borrowed musical theme or a copied camera framing carries the reference with no words at all. Cue: ask 'what earlier text am I being reminded of, and through which mode?'

questions.stem: A road safety television advertisement films a teenage driver using the shaky handheld camera, green night-vision tint and heavy breathing of a well-known horror film. This intertextual choice most likely works by:
options: transferring the dread the audience associates with horror onto an everyday drive home
proving that driving at night is statistically more dangerous than driving in daylight
reassuring viewers that the situation is fictional, so the warning feels less confronting
showing that the advertisement was made by the same team as the horror film
questions.explanation: Borrowing the visual and audio conventions of horror imports the emotional response those conventions already trigger, so an ordinary drive is reframed as a threat — that emotional transfer is the point of the reference. The reassurance option reverses the effect: horror conventions heighten tension rather than defuse it. Note also that borrowed style is never evidence of shared authorship or of statistical claims.

questions.stem: Two students analyse a music video that recreates famous shots from a 1980s teen film, but casts the outsider character as the hero and the popular group as ridiculous. Which analysis best explains how the intertextual reference layers meaning?
options: The reference removes the original film's meaning and replaces it with a straightforward tribute to the 1980s
The recreated shots invite comparison, and the changed roles use that comparison to criticise the original's values
The recreated shots show the artist could not think of original imagery, so the video has little meaning of its own
The reference is only decorative, since audiences who missed the 1980s film still enjoy the video's editing
questions.explanation: When a text copies recognisable shots but alters who is admired, the audience's memory of the original becomes the measuring stick, and the changes read as commentary — this is how a reference can critique as well as honour. The 'only decorative' option is tempting because some viewers do miss the reference, but a device can still carry meaning for informed viewers while remaining watchable for others. Cue: look for what has been changed, not just what has been copied.

questions.stem: In your English classes, 'academic vocabulary' is best described as:
options: general words used across school subjects to explain, analyse and connect ideas precisely
slang words and abbreviations that students use to take down notes quickly in class
the longest words available in a dictionary, chosen mainly to make writing sound impressive
words that belong to one subject only and are never used in writing for any other subject
questions.explanation: Academic vocabulary is the shared set of formal, mostly abstract words (analyse, significant, consequently, factor) that writers in many subjects use to name ideas and show how they relate. The option about words belonging to one subject only describes discipline-specific technical terms, and even those are not banned from other subjects, so the claim is false. The cue: academic vocabulary travels between subjects, while technical vocabulary names the content of a particular field.

questions.stem: Which sentence rewrites 'The author reckons heaps of people are dodgy about climate science' in appropriate academic vocabulary?
options: The author argues that many people remain sceptical about climate science.
The author reckons that a significant proportion of people are dodgy about climate science.
The author, in essence, reckons heaps of individuals distrust the field of climate science.
The author's view is that people are super unconvinced regarding the climate science area.
questions.explanation: Academic register needs consistently formal choices: 'argues' replaces 'reckons' and 'sceptical' replaces 'dodgy'. The version with 'a significant proportion' is tempting because it sounds formal, but it still keeps 'reckons' and 'dodgy', so the register is mixed rather than academic. Check every word in a rewrite, not just the one you changed.

questions.stem: Why do teachers ask for academic vocabulary in an analytical essay?
options: It allows the writer to discuss a topic without ever committing to a position
It states ideas precisely and keeps the tone impersonal, which suits a formal reader
It automatically earns higher marks because longer words impress any marker
It removes the need to support claims with quotations and detail from the text
questions.explanation: The role of academic vocabulary is precision and objectivity: words like 'implies', 'contributes to' or 'consequently' name ideas and relationships exactly, without chatty or emotional colouring. The claim about longer words impressing markers is the common trap, but a long word used inaccurately weakens writing rather than improving it. Ask whether the word is the most exact one, not the biggest one.

questions.stem: Academic writing often uses nominalisation, turning actions into nouns. Which sentence does this?
options: The destruction of the wetland continued for several decades.
The wetland was destroyed by developers over several decades.
Developers destroyed the wetland across several long decades.
The wetland kept being destroyed, decade after decade, sadly.
questions.explanation: Nominalisation packs a process into a noun group: the action 'destroy' becomes the noun 'destruction', which can then act as the subject of the sentence. The passive sentence 'was destroyed by developers' is tempting because it also sounds formal, but the action is still a verb, so no nominalisation has occurred. Look for the noun form of the action (-tion, -ment, -ance, -ity) sitting where a doer would normally go.

questions.stem: A student must report a trend without overstating it: 'This graph ___ that recycling rates have improved.' Which choice is appropriate academic vocabulary?
options: proves beyond doubt
reckons
totally confirms
suggests
questions.explanation: Academic vocabulary includes hedging verbs such as 'suggests', 'indicates' and 'implies', which report evidence without claiming more than the data can support. 'Proves beyond doubt' is the tempting distractor because it sounds confident and formal, but a single graph cannot establish certainty, so the claim is overstated. When you write about evidence, match the strength of the verb to the strength of the proof.

questions.stem: 'Sea levels rose along the coast. ___, several councils invested in flood barriers.' Which academic connective correctly signals the relationship between the two ideas?
options: In contrast
Consequently
Nevertheless
For instance
questions.explanation: The second sentence states a result of the first, so a cause-and-effect connective such as 'consequently' or 'therefore' is required. 'Nevertheless' is the most tempting alternative because it also sounds formal, but it signals a contrast or concession, which misrepresents the link between rising seas and building barriers. Decide the logical relationship first, then select the connective that names it.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Shakespeare utilises juxtaposition to illustrate conflict, which is pretty full-on and makes the reader go wow.' What is the most accurate evaluation of the vocabulary here?
options: The academic terms are undercut by colloquial phrases, so the register becomes inconsistent
The sentence is appropriate because it contains two accurate academic terms already
The main fault is 'utilises', because academic writing avoids verbs with Latin origins
The main fault is mentioning the reader, because academic writing never refers to audience
questions.explanation: Academic vocabulary works only when the register is sustained; 'juxtaposition' and 'illustrate' are appropriate, but 'pretty full-on' and 'go wow' drag the sentence into casual speech. The option defending the sentence because it has two accurate terms is tempting, but correct terminology does not cancel out slang. Read your sentence for any phrase you would only say aloud to a friend.

questions.stem: In English, some academic words are general (useful in almost any subject) while others are discipline-specific (belonging to the study of texts). Which word is discipline-specific?
options: enjambment
significant
evaluate
factor
questions.explanation: Discipline-specific academic vocabulary names concepts belonging to one field of study; 'enjambment' only has meaning when analysing poetry, where it names a line running on without end punctuation. 'Evaluate' is tempting because it sounds academic and appears in English tasks, but it is a general academic verb used in science, history and maths reports as well, so it is not specific to text study. The cue is to ask whether a geography or science teacher would use the word in the same sense: if yes, it is general academic vocabulary.
questions.teaching:
Academic vocabulary splits into two kinds, and the distinction matters when you are learning subject terminology.

General academic words are useful across every subject — analyse, evaluate, significant, demonstrate, factor. Discipline-specific words belong to one field and mean little outside it. In English, that second group includes the technical terms of literary study: the names for verse structure, sound devices and dramatic conventions. Testing a word means asking whether it would be useful in a science report as well as an essay.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written in an appropriate academic register for an English essay?
options: The novel is basically about how loyalty in wartime is kind of pointless
The novel, to be honest, gets you asking if loyalty even matters in war
The novel positions readers to question the value of loyalty in wartime
The novel really makes you think twice about being loyal in a war
questions.explanation: Academic register uses precise, impersonal wording and analytical verbs such as 'positions', which names what the text does to readers. 'Really makes you think twice' is tempting because it states an effect on the reader, but the second-person 'you' and the colloquial phrasing belong to conversation, not essay writing. Scan your sentences for 'you', 'basically', 'kind of' and 'to be honest' — these are reliable signals that the register has slipped.

questions.stem: A student wants to report that a journalist attacks a government policy in very strong terms. Which reporting verb best conveys this in academic vocabulary?
options: talks about
condemns
mentions
reckons
questions.explanation: Reporting verbs carry information about strength and stance, and 'condemns' precisely names forceful criticism. 'Mentions' is the trap for students hunting a formal-sounding word: it signals a brief passing reference and therefore misreports the journalist's strong attack. Choose the reporting verb that matches the intensity and attitude of the source, not simply the one that sounds neutral or safe.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'I reckon the poem shows me that memory hurts, and I think that's really sad.' Which revision keeps the claim but shifts it into academic vocabulary?
options: The poem made me feel really sad about how much memory hurts
The poem represents memory as a source of enduring pain
The poem, in my personal opinion, is quite a sad poem about memory
I strongly believe the poem proves that all memories are painful
questions.explanation: Academic vocabulary keeps the focus on the text rather than the writer's feelings, using analytical verbs like 'represents' and abstract nouns like 'pain' to make an arguable claim. 'I strongly believe the poem proves that all memories are painful' is tempting because it sounds forceful, but it keeps first-person opinion phrasing and overstates with 'proves' and 'all'. The cue: an academic sentence should be able to start with the text as its subject.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The poem infers that grief never really ends.' A teacher marks the word 'infers'. What is the problem?
options: Poems cannot make claims at all, so no analytical verb belongs in this sentence
'Infers' is only used for spoken language, so 'states' should be used for written texts
Texts imply meanings while readers infer them, so 'implies' or 'suggests' is needed here
'Infers' is too informal for an essay and should be replaced with a longer academic synonym
questions.explanation: 'Imply' and 'infer' name opposite ends of the same process: a text implies a meaning, and a reader draws an inference from it. Calling the word 'too informal' is the tempting response because students associate marked words with slang, but 'infer' is fully academic — it is simply pointing the wrong way. Remember the direction: writers and texts imply, audiences infer.

questions.stem: A student replaces 'The writer uses lots of describing words' in an essay. Which revision uses academic vocabulary to add precision rather than only to sound formal?
options: The writer deploys, in my view, many highly descriptive terms here
The writer accumulates sensory adjectives to build a claustrophobic setting
The writer employs an abundance of describing words in this section
The writer utilises a plethora of vocabulary items right throughout
questions.explanation: Academic vocabulary earns its place when technical terms make a claim sharper: 'sensory adjectives' names the word class and its effect, and 'claustrophobic setting' names the result. 'Employs an abundance of describing words' is the closest trap — it swaps in formal synonyms but still says nothing more than the original sentence did. Test each upgraded word by asking what extra information it gives the reader; if the answer is none, it is decoration.

questions.stem: Using academic vocabulary accurately matters as much as using it at all. Which sentence uses a discipline-specific term with its correct meaning?
options: A text's protagonist is the character who opposes the hero's goals.
A text's stanza is the line that repeats at the end of each verse.
A text's tone is the order in which the writer arranges the events.
A text's thesis is the central argument the writer sets out to defend.
questions.explanation: In the study of texts, a thesis is the controlling claim or argument that the rest of the writing supports, so that definition is accurate. The most tempting error is the sentence about the protagonist, because it swaps in the definition of the antagonist — the protagonist is the central character whose goals drive the text. The other two confuse a stanza (a grouped set of lines in a poem) with a refrain, and tone (the writer's attitude) with plot or structure. Cue: before you use an academic term in an essay, check you could define it in your own words, since a misused term weakens the analysis more than a plain word would.

questions.stem: Which spelling of the technical term for words that imitate sounds (such as 'crash' or 'buzz') is correct?
options: onomatopeia
onomatapoeia
onomotopoeia
onomatopoeia
questions.explanation: The term is built from Greek parts and is spelled onomatopoeia, ending with the 'oe' pairing in -poeia; a useful memory chunk is on-o-mat-o-poe-ia. The most tempting error is onomatopeia, which drops the 'o' from the -poeia ending because that sound is not clearly heard when the word is said aloud. Say the word slowly in six chunks and check that the final chunk is spelled 'poe-ia'.
questions.teaching:
This term names words that imitate the sound they describe — crash, buzz, hiss, splash.

It is one of the hardest literary words to spell, and breaking it into its Greek roots helps: 'onoma' meaning name, and 'poiein' meaning to make. So it is literally sound-name-making. Written out, that gives the unusual run of vowels in the middle that people tend to guess at. Writing the roots and then joining them is more reliable than trying to remember the whole string.

questions.stem: Which spelling of the poetic device term meaning the repetition of initial consonant sounds is correct?
options: alliteraton
aliterration
alliteration
aliteration
questions.explanation: Alliteration keeps the double l from the Latin prefix ad- joined to littera (letter), then ends with the common noun suffix -ation. The trap is aliteration, which uses a single l because only one l sound is heard when the word is spoken. Remember that the double letter is in the same place as in 'illustrate' and 'illuminate': prefix plus doubled consonant.
questions.teaching:
Literary terminology is worth learning to spell as well as to define, because misspelling it in an essay undermines the analysis.

This one comes from the Latin for 'letter' and describes repeating the sound at the start of nearby words. The spelling trap is the double letter in the middle — it has two Ls, following the pattern of 'allocate' and 'allude', where the prefix ad- has assimilated into the following consonant. Saying the word slowly while writing it out is the practical fix.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The poet ___ names the river in the final line.' Which spelling of the adverb formed from 'specific' is correct?
options: specifically
specificly
specificaly
specifiaclly
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -ic form their adverb by adding -ally, so specific becomes specifically, just as basic becomes basically and dramatic becomes dramatically. The tempting error is specificly, which adds only -ly because that matches the sound of the spoken word. Cue: if the adjective ends in -ic, write -ally, not -ly.
questions.teaching:
Adverbs are usually formed by adding -ly to an adjective, and the spelling depends on how the adjective ends.

Where the adjective already ends in -ic, English inserts -al before -ly: so the pattern runs basic to basically, dramatic to dramatically, scientific to scientifically. That extra syllable is easy to miss when writing quickly, because it is often swallowed in speech. Learning the -ic to -ically rule covers a large family of words at once, which is why it is worth knowing as a rule rather than word by word.

questions.stem: 'This essay compares three ___ of the same poem.' Which form correctly completes the sentence?
options: analysis
analysies
analyses
analysises
questions.explanation: Academic words taken from Greek that end in -sis form their plural by changing -sis to -ses, so analysis becomes analyses, as basis becomes bases and hypothesis becomes hypotheses. The word analysis is tempting, but it is singular and cannot follow 'three'. Cue: -sis for one, -ses for more than one.

questions.stem: 'In this stanza the ___ of the storm is unusually detailed.' Which spelling of the noun formed from 'describe' is correct?
options: descripsion
description
discription
describtion
questions.explanation: When describe becomes a noun, the b changes to p and the ending is -tion: description. The most tempting error is discription, because the first unstressed vowel sounds like a short i, but the word keeps the de- prefix of describe and describes. Cue: link the spelling back to 'describe' for the de-, then remember the p and the -tion ending.

questions.stem: 'The poem's strongest ___ on the reader is a feeling of unease.' Which word correctly completes the sentence?
options: efect
affext
effect
affect
questions.explanation: Here the missing word is a noun following 'strongest', and the noun meaning result or impact is effect. The temptation is affect, which in everyday academic writing is a verb meaning to influence, as in 'the imagery affects the reader'. Cue: if you can put 'the' or an adjective in front of it, you need the noun effect.

questions.stem: Which pair of academic words is spelled correctly?
options: refered / reference
referred / reference
refered / referrence
referred / referrence
questions.explanation: In referred the stress stays on the final syllable of 'refer', so the r doubles before the vowel suffix; in reference the stress shifts back to the first syllable, so the r is not doubled. The most tempting choice pairs the correct referred with referrence, applying the doubling rule to a word where the stress has moved. Cue: say the word aloud — re-FERRED doubles, REF-erence does not.

questions.stem: Which sentence has every technical term spelled correctly?
options: The playwright uses soliloquy and dramatic irony to build tension.
The playwrite uses soliloquy and dramatic irony to build tension.
The playwright uses solilaquy and dramatic irony to build tension.
The playwright uses soliloquy and dramatic irony to build tention.
questions.explanation: Playwright uses the old word 'wright', meaning maker (as in shipwright), soliloquy keeps the -quy ending, and tension ends in -sion. The most tempting error is playwrite, because a playwright writes plays, but the word has never contained 'write'. Cue: a wright makes things, and tension follows the same -sion pattern as extension.

questions.stem: Which spelling of the technical term for giving human qualities to something non-human is correct?
options: personification
personifaction
personnification
personifacation
questions.explanation: The term is built from 'person' + 'ify' (to make into) + '-cation' pattern, giving per-son-i-fi-ca-tion: personification. The version with 'faction' in the middle is the most tempting because it borrows the familiar word 'faction', but the base here is 'personify', so the letters after 'personi' must be 'fication'. Say the word slowly in syllables and check that you can hear 'fy' becoming 'fi-ca-tion'; also remember 'person' has only one n.
questions.teaching:
This term describes giving human qualities to something non-human, and its spelling follows a regular English pattern.

The root is 'person', and the ending is the standard '-ification' seen in 'identification', 'classification' and 'simplification'. Building it from those two pieces gives the spelling without guesswork. The trap is the vowel joining them — English uses -ific- rather than -efic-, consistently across this whole family of words. Recognising the pattern means you can spell all of them, not just this one.

questions.stem: Which spelling of the drama term for a speech in which a character alone on stage voices their thoughts is correct?
options: solilaquy
soliloquey
soliliquy
soliloquy
questions.explanation: Soliloquy comes from Latin roots meaning 'alone' (solus) and 'speak' (loqui), and the '-loquy' ending appears in related words such as 'colloquial' and 'eloquent'. The version ending in '-loquey' is the most tempting, because students expect an 'ey' ending to match the way the word sounds, but the Latin ending is '-quy'. Link it to 'colloquial' in your notes: same '-loqu-' chunk, so the vowels before it stay as o-i-lo.
questions.teaching:
Drama terminology often comes from Latin or Italian, and the spellings follow those origins rather than English phonetics.

This term combines the Latin roots for 'alone' and 'speak', which is exactly what the device is: a character alone on stage, voicing their thoughts. Knowing the roots fixes the beginning of the spelling. The ending follows the same pattern as 'colloquy' and 'obloquy', all from the same Latin verb for speaking. Related words like 'soliloquise' keep the same stem.

questions.stem: 'Her ___ of the poem's imagery is detailed, and she ___ each stanza in turn.' Which pair correctly completes the sentence?
options: analysis … analysis
analyses … analyses
analysis … analyses
analyses … analysis
questions.explanation: 'Analysis' is the singular noun (a thing you produce), while 'analyses' here is the verb form used with 'she'. The first gap follows 'Her', so a noun is needed; the second gap needs a verb to match the subject 'she'. Reversing them is tempting because 'analyses' can also be the plural noun, but a plural noun cannot follow 'Her … is detailed', and 'analysis' can never act as a verb. Cue: if the word is doing something, it takes the -ses ending; if it is a thing, it ends -sis.

questions.stem: An essay needs the words made by adding -ing and -ence to 'refer'. Which pair is spelled correctly?
options: refering … referrence
referring … reference
refering … reference
referring … referrence
questions.explanation: In 'refer' the stress falls on the last syllable, so the final r doubles before the vowel suffix: referring. When '-ence' is added the stress shifts back to the first syllable ('REF-erence'), so the r is not doubled. The pair with 'referring' and 'referrence' is the trap, because it assumes the doubling rule applies to every suffix rather than depending on where the stress lands. Say each word aloud: if you stress 'fer', double the r; if you stress 'ref', keep one r.

questions.stem: A review calls a film "relentless". What does that suggest?
options: It repeats the same scene often
It was difficult to make
It never lets up in pace or intensity
It is longer than it needs to be
questions.explanation: Relentless describes something that does not pause or soften. Whether it reads as praise or criticism depends on the sentence around it.

questions.stem: Which word has the most negative connotation?
options: Resolute
Stubborn
Determined
Persistent
questions.explanation: All four describe someone who will not change their mind, but only stubborn implies it is unreasonable. Connotation is the attitude a word carries beyond its meaning.

questions.stem: A character is described as "sauntering" into a room. What does this suggest?
options: A slow, painful movement
An unhurried, confident walk
A nervous, hurried entrance
A noisy, clumsy arrival
questions.explanation: Saunter carries ease and a certain self-assurance. Writers choose between walk, stride, shuffle and saunter precisely for these shades.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses "affect" correctly?
options: The weather will affect the match
The weather will have an affect
The affect of the news was clear
She affects were noticeable
questions.explanation: Affect is almost always the verb and effect the noun. Substituting "influence" is a quick test: if it fits, affect is the word.

questions.stem: What is a homophone?
options: A word that sounds the same but is spelled differently
A word with more than one meaning
A word spelled the same but said differently
A word borrowed from another language
questions.explanation: Their, there and they are all sound alike but mean different things. A spellchecker cannot catch a homophone error, which is why they persist.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling?
options: Separate
Seperate
Seperete
Separete
questions.explanation: There is a rat in the middle of separate, which is the standard way of remembering it. It is one of the most commonly misspelled words in English.

questions.stem: What does the prefix "mis" mean in misinterpret?
options: Before
Against
Wrongly
Again
questions.explanation: Mis means wrongly or badly, as in misread and misjudge. Knowing a handful of prefixes unlocks the meaning of many unfamiliar words.

questions.stem: What does the suffix "less" do in "hopeless"?
options: It means without
It means full of
It means smaller
It makes the word a verb
questions.explanation: Less turns a noun into an adjective meaning without it. The opposite suffix is ful, as in hopeful.

questions.stem: A writer describes a city as "a wound that never closes". What is this?
options: Alliteration
A metaphor
A simile
Personification
questions.explanation: It states the city is a wound rather than saying it is like one, which is what makes it a metaphor. A simile would need like or as.

questions.stem: What is the effect of a short sentence after several long ones?
options: It signals a new character
It makes the writing formal
It lands with emphasis
It slows the pace down
questions.explanation: Contrast in sentence length creates emphasis, and the short one draws the eye. Sentence length is a deliberate choice, not an accident.

questions.stem: Which word is most formal?
options: Get
Grab
Purchase
Buy
questions.explanation: All four mean the same action, but they sit at different levels of formality. Matching the register to the audience is the skill being tested.

questions.stem: A text uses "we" and "our" throughout. What is the likely effect?
options: It makes the writing more objective
It signals the writer is uncertain
It marks the text as fiction
It includes the reader in a shared position
questions.explanation: Inclusive pronouns invite the reader onto the writer side of an argument, which is why persuasive writing uses them so often.

questions.stem: What does "ambiguous" mean?
options: Difficult to pronounce
Very old fashioned
Deliberately offensive
Open to more than one meaning
questions.explanation: An ambiguous sentence can be read two ways, which is sometimes a fault and sometimes the point. Writers use it deliberately in poetry.

questions.stem: Which spelling rule explains "hoping" losing its e?
options: Change the y to an i
Add k before ing
Drop the silent e before a vowel suffix
Double the last letter before ing
questions.explanation: Hope becomes hoping but hop becomes hopping, and the difference is what happens to the silent e. The rule explains a whole family of words.

questions.stem: Why might a writer repeat a word three times in a row?
options: To fill space on the page
To show the character is confused
Because synonyms were unavailable
To build emphasis and rhythm
questions.explanation: Deliberate repetition creates rhythm and drives a point home, and it is a standard persuasive technique. Accidental repetition reads very differently.

questions.stem: What is the tone of a text that uses short, blunt sentences and plain words?
options: Whimsical
Ornate
Direct
Nostalgic
questions.explanation: Tone comes from word choice and sentence structure together. Long sentences with elaborate vocabulary would give a very different impression.

questions.stem: Which is an antonym of "generous"?
options: Charitable
Lavish
Giving
Miserly
questions.explanation: An antonym is an opposite, and miserly is the only option that means unwilling to give. The other three are near synonyms.

questions.stem: A speech says "this is not merely unfair, it is unjust". What is the effect of "merely"?
options: It shows the speaker is unsure
It marks the sentence as a question
It escalates the claim to something stronger
It softens the accusation
questions.explanation: Merely dismisses the first word as not going far enough, so the second lands harder. Escalation like this is common in persuasive speech.

questions.stem: What does the word "context" mean in English study?
options: The main character of a text
The number of words in a text
The circumstances a text was made or read in
The plot of a text
questions.explanation: Context covers when, where and for whom a text was created, and it shapes how it is understood. The same text can read differently in another decade.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
options: The dogs lead's was missing
The dog's lead was missing
The dog's were barking loudly
Its' lead was missing
questions.explanation: An apostrophe shows possession or a missing letter, never a plural. The lead belongs to the dog, so the apostrophe goes before the s.

questions.stem: A writer uses technical terms without explaining them. What does that suggest?
options: The text is fiction
The text is written for an expert audience
The writer is unsure of the topic
The text is meant for children
questions.explanation: Assumed knowledge is a strong signal about the intended reader. A general audience would need those terms defined or replaced.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a synonym and a homonym?
options: Both are spelling rules
Synonyms share meaning, homonyms share form
Synonyms share form, homonyms share meaning
Both share meaning exactly
questions.explanation: Big and large are synonyms, while bat the animal and bat the sports equipment are homonyms. The words look alike but describe opposite relationships.
